title: Open channel flow: free surfaces, the Froude number and critical depth
examples: How do you calculate the Froude number?
What is critical depth in a channel?

explain.say: Rivers, irrigation canals, roadside drains and even sewers share one thing: the water has a free surface, open to the air. That is open channel flow, and it behaves quite differently from water in a full pipe. Let us compare the two on the board.

explain.say: In a pipe, pressure pushes the water along and the pipe stays full. In an open channel only gravity moves it, sliding down the slope of the bed, and the depth can rise and fall. So depth becomes a key unknown. What sets how fast a canal flows: its slope, or a pump's pressure?

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: A free surface makes depth a key unknown

explain.say: Its slope! Now the key number in channels, the Froude number: velocity over the square root of g times depth. It compares the flow speed with the speed of a small surface wave. Below one is subcritical, deep and calm; above one is supercritical, shallow and fast. Water at three metres per second, half a metre deep, has a Froude number of about one point three five.

So that flow is supercritical. Here is why critical matters. Specific energy is depth plus velocity head, the energy the flow carries above the bed. For two cubic metres per second per metre width, it has a lowest point at the critical depth, zero point seven four metres. Any higher energy allows two depths: one deep and slow, one shallow and fast.

draw.text: Minimum specific energy E = 1.5 y_c ≈ 1.11 m

explain.say: That is why weirs and flumes can measure flow: at a crest the water passes through critical depth, so one depth reading gives the discharge. Brilliant! Exam tip: find the Froude number first, because it tells you which way disturbances travel. Challenge: is a flow one metre deep at two metres per second subcritical or supercritical?

faq.a: Flow with a free surface open to the air, driven by gravity, as in rivers, canals, culverts and part-full sewers. The depth can change, unlike flow in a full pipe.
The Froude number is velocity divided by the square root of g times depth. It compares the flow speed with the speed of small surface waves; 3 metres per second at 0.5 metres deep gives about 1.35.

faq.q: What is the difference between subcritical and supercritical flow?
faq.a: Subcritical flow, Froude number below 1, is deep and slow, and waves can travel upstream. Supercritical flow, above 1, is shallow and fast, and waves are swept downstream.

Critical depth is the depth at which a given flow has its minimum specific energy and a Froude number of exactly 1. In a rectangular channel it is the cube root of q squared over g: 0.74 metres for 2 cubic metres per second per metre.
asks: How do you calculate critical depth?

faq.a: Specific energy is the flow depth plus the velocity head, V squared over 2g, measured from the channel bed. Plotted against depth it gives a curve with a minimum at critical depth.

facts: In a rectangular channel, critical depth is y_c = (q²/g)^(1/3) and the minimum specific energy is 1.5 y_c.
The Froude number is named after William Froude, a 19th-century English engineer famous for testing ship models.

quiz.say: Water flows one metre deep at two metres per second. What is the Froude number?

wrong.1: That forgets the square root of g times depth.
wrong.2: That divides by g itself instead of its square root times depth.

quiz.say: At critical depth, the specific energy is…
quiz.show: At critical depth, the specific energy is…
quiz.why: Critical depth is the lowest point of the specific energy curve.

wrong.1: The curve has no maximum; energy grows for very shallow and very deep flow.
wrong.2: Moving water always carries some energy above the bed.
